title: "Module 8 — Bivariate I: contingency tables and scatter plots"
subtitle: "Data Description | Part III — Two variables and synthesis"
date-modified: 2026-10-17
lang: en
---

**The business question.** Every univariate indicator so far described
**one** variable at a time. The real question behind "The Wandering
Fork"'s trading is whether two variables move together — does warmer
weather really bring more revenue? Do promotions work better on sunny
days? This module introduces the two graphical tools for answering
that: the contingency table (for two qualitative-or-grouped variables)
and the scatter plot (for two quantitative variables). We start with a
table and five days small enough to handle by hand, and only then
write the notation.

## Learning objectives

By the end of this module, you will be able to:

- Build a contingency table by hand from a list of individuals, and
  read a cell count $n_{ij}$ and the margins $n_{i\cdot}$, $n_{\cdot j}$
  aloud.
- Compute row and column marginal distributions from a contingency
  table, as $n_{i\cdot}/n$ and $n_{\cdot j}/n$.
- Compute a **conditional distribution** — the distribution of one
  variable restricted to a single modality of the other — and use it
  to compare sub-groups fairly.
- Read a share such as $n_{ij}/n_{i\cdot}$ aloud as a sentence, and
  write a share described in words in this notation.
- Draw a scatter plot of two quantitative variables by hand and
  describe the pattern it shows (direction, form, exceptions).
- Distinguish "a visible pattern" from "a proven relationship" —
  formalised numerically in Module 9.

## Theory

### Sun, rain and medium days

One Wandering Fork truck classified 50 of its trading days by weather
(keeping only Sunny and Rainy days) and by revenue level: **Low**
(under €500), **Medium** (€500 to under €700) and **High** (€700 or
more). The numbers are a simplified extract chosen so that you can
compute everything by hand.

| Weather \ Revenue | Low | Medium | High |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Sunny | 3 | 9 | 18 |
| Rainy | 12 | 6 | 2 |

The truck had **9 medium days when it was sunny, and only 6 when it
rained**. Is a medium day more likely when the sun is out? And what
would you tell the owner about High days: is "18 against 2" the right
way to compare sunny and rainy weather?

### Contingency table

Where does a table like the one above come from? From a plain list of
days, each one described by **two** variables at once.

**Try it.** Here are ten days of the same truck's log. Tally them into
the table below, then add the row and column totals. Number the rows
$i = 1$ (Sunny), $i = 2$ (Rainy) and the columns $j = 1$ (Low),
$j = 2$ (Medium), $j = 3$ (High).

| Day | Weather | Revenue level |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Sunny | High |
| 2 | Sunny | Medium |
| 3 | Rainy | Low |
| 4 | Sunny | High |
| 5 | Rainy | Medium |
| 6 | Sunny | Low |
| 7 | Sunny | High |
| 8 | Rainy | Low |
| 9 | Sunny | Medium |
| 10 | Rainy | High |

| Weather \ Revenue | Low | Medium | High | Row total |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Sunny | ? | ? | ? | ? |
| Rainy | ? | ? | ? | ? |
| **Column total** | **?** | **?** | **?** | **?** |

1. How many days were Sunny **and** High?
2. Count the Sunny days in the log directly, ignoring revenue. Do you
   get the Sunny row total?

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
#### Try it — check your answer
| Weather \ Revenue | Low | Medium | High | Row total |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Sunny | 1 | 2 | 3 | 6 |
| Rainy | 2 | 1 | 1 | 4 |
| **Column total** | **3** | **3** | **4** | **10** |

1. 3 days (Days 1, 4 and 7) were Sunny and High.
2. Yes: the log has 6 Sunny days, which is the Sunny row total. Each
   day lands in exactly one cell, so the ten days fill the six cells
   and every total adds up to 10.
:::

**See it.** Each day is one dot in exactly one cell — the cell where
its row (weather) and its column (revenue level) cross:

| Weather \ Revenue | Low | Medium | High |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sunny | ● (Day 6) | ●● (Days 2, 9) | ●●● (Days 1, 4, 7) |
| Rainy | ●● (Days 3, 8) | ● (Day 5) | ● (Day 10) |

In plain words: a contingency table is a two-dimensional frequency
table. The margins are the row and column totals — they give you back
the one-variable frequency tables you already know.

::: {.callout-note}
#### Definition — contingency table
A **contingency table** (or cross-tabulation) crosses the modalities
of two variables observed on the same individuals: cell $(i,j)$ holds
the count $n_{ij}$ of individuals with modality $i$ of the first
variable **and** modality $j$ of the second. The **row margin**
$n_{i\cdot} = \sum_j n_{ij}$ and **column margin**
$n_{\cdot j} = \sum_i n_{ij}$ recover each variable's own (univariate)
frequency table from the same data.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
#### Notation decoder — contingency table
| Symbol | Read aloud | In our example (ten days) |
|---|---|---|
| $(i,j)$ | "cell i, j" — row first, then column | $(1,3)$ is the Sunny–High cell |
| $n_{ij}$ | "n sub i j" | $n_{13} = 3$ Sunny and High days |
| $n_{i\cdot}$ | "n sub i dot" — the dot replaces the index that was added up | $n_{1\cdot} = 6$ Sunny days |
| $n_{\cdot j}$ | "n sub dot j" | $n_{\cdot 3} = 4$ High days |
| $\sum_j$ | "add up over all columns j" | across a row: $1+2+3 = 6$ |
| $\sum_i$ | "add up over all rows i" | down a column: $3+1 = 4$ |

**Whole formula as a sentence:** "the row margin $n_{i\cdot}$ is the
sum of the counts across row $i$; the column margin $n_{\cdot j}$ is
the sum of the counts down column $j$." Adding all the cells gives the
grand total $n = 10$.
:::

### Marginal distributions

**Try it.** Go back to the 50-day table of the hook. Complete the
totals, then turn each total into a share of all 50 days.

| Weather \ Revenue | Low | Medium | High | Row total | % of all days |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Sunny | 3 | 9 | 18 | ? | ? |
| Rainy | 12 | 6 | 2 | ? | ? |
| **Column total** | **?** | **?** | **?** | **50** | |
| **% of all days** | **?** | **?** | **?** | | **100%** |

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
#### Try it — check your answer
| Weather \ Revenue | Low | Medium | High | Row total | % of all days |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Sunny | 3 | 9 | 18 | 30 | 60% |
| Rainy | 12 | 6 | 2 | 20 | 40% |
| **Column total** | **15** | **15** | **20** | **50** | |
| **% of all days** | **30%** | **30%** | **40%** | | **100%** |

The truck had 30 Sunny days ($30/50 = 60\%$) and 20 Rainy days
($40\%$). Separately, 40% of all days were High. Notice that Sunny days
are simply **more numerous** — this already explains part of
"9 against 6".
:::

**See it.** The two margins are two ordinary one-variable bar charts
(each block = 10% of the 50 days):

| Variable | Modality | Share of all 50 days |
|---|---|---|
| Weather (row margin) | Sunny | ██████ 60% |
| | Rainy | ████ 40% |
| Revenue (column margin) | Low | ███ 30% |
| | Medium | ███ 30% |
| | High | ████ 40% |

**Recall.** In [Module 2](module-02.qmd) you computed relative
frequencies $f_i = n_i/n$ for one variable. A marginal distribution is
exactly that, using the margins of the table as the counts.

In plain words: a marginal distribution is the share of all $n$
individuals in each modality of one variable, read off the edge of the
table — as if the other variable did not exist.

::: {.callout-tip}
#### Formula — marginal distributions
Dividing each margin by the grand total $n$ gives the two **marginal
distributions** (relative frequencies, as in Module 2):
$$
\frac{n_{i\cdot}}{n} \quad \text{(row variable)}, \qquad
\frac{n_{\cdot j}}{n} \quad \text{(column variable)}.
$$
Each one sums to 1 (100%) and ignores the other variable entirely.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
#### Notation decoder — marginal distributions
| Symbol | Read aloud | In our example (50 days) |
|---|---|---|
| $n$ | "n" | 50 days |
| $n_{i\cdot}$ | "n sub i dot" | row totals: $n_{1\cdot} = 30$, $n_{2\cdot} = 20$ |
| $n_{\cdot j}$ | "n sub dot j" | column totals: 15, 15, 20 |
| $\frac{n_{i\cdot}}{n}$ | "n sub i dot over n" | $30/50 = 60\%$ Sunny, $20/50 = 40\%$ Rainy |
| $\frac{n_{\cdot j}}{n}$ | "n sub dot j over n" | $15/50 = 30\%$, 30%, $20/50 = 40\%$ |

**Whole formula as a sentence:** "the marginal share of a modality is
its row (or column) total divided by the grand total."
:::

### Conditional distribution

**Try it.** To answer the hook, compute percentages **within each
row**: divide every cell by its own row total (30 for Sunny, 20 for
Rainy), not by 50.

| Weather \ Revenue | Low | Medium | High | Total |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Sunny ($\div 30$) | ? | ? | ? | 100% |
| Rainy ($\div 20$) | ? | ? | ? | 100% |
| All days ($\div 50$) | 30% | 30% | 40% | 100% |

1. Is a medium day more likely when it is sunny?
2. How do High days compare between the two kinds of weather?
3. Now read **down** the High column instead: of the 20 High days,
   what share were Sunny?

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
#### Try it — check your answer
| Weather \ Revenue | Low | Medium | High | Total |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Sunny ($\div 30$) | 10% | 30% | 60% | 100% |
| Rainy ($\div 20$) | 60% | 30% | 10% | 100% |
| All days ($\div 50$) | 30% | 30% | 40% | 100% |

1. No: $9/30 = 30\%$ and $6/20 = 30\%$. "9 against 6" only reflects
   that there were more Sunny days.
2. $18/30 = 60\%$ of Sunny days were High, against $2/20 = 10\%$ of
   Rainy days: here the weather really makes a difference.
3. $18/20 = 90\%$ of High days were Sunny. This is a different
   question ("given High") from question 2 ("given Sunny"), so it has
   a different answer.
:::

**See it.** Each row now has its own 100% bar (each block = 10% of
that row):

| Given | Low | Medium | High |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sunny | █ 10% | ███ 30% | ██████ 60% |
| Rainy | ██████ 60% | ███ 30% | █ 10% |
| All days (marginal) | ███ 30% | ███ 30% | ████ 40% |

The Medium column is identical in all three rows; the Low and High
columns are not — that is where weather and revenue are associated.

In plain words: to compare Sunny vs Rainy days fairly, don't compare
raw counts (Sunny has more days total). Instead, compute percentages
*within* each weather type — that's the conditional distribution.

::: {.callout-note}
#### Definition — conditional distribution
A **conditional distribution** is the distribution of one variable
*restricted* to a single modality of the other — one row (or one
column), rescaled to its own row (or column) total instead of the
grand total $n$. It answers "given this category, how is the other
variable distributed?", which the raw counts alone cannot, since row
totals differ in size.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
#### Formula — conditional distributions
Given row modality $i$, the share of column modality $j$ is
$$
\frac{n_{ij}}{n_{i\cdot}} \quad \text{(row percentages)},
$$
and given column modality $j$, the share of row modality $i$ is
$$
\frac{n_{ij}}{n_{\cdot j}} \quad \text{(column percentages)}.
$$
Each conditional distribution sums to 1 (100%) over its own row (or
column).
:::

::: {.callout-note}
#### Notation decoder — conditional distributions
| Symbol | Read aloud | In our example (50 days) |
|---|---|---|
| $n_{ij}$ | "n sub i j" | $n_{13} = 18$ Sunny and High days |
| $n_{i\cdot}$ | "n sub i dot" | $n_{1\cdot} = 30$ Sunny days |
| $n_{\cdot j}$ | "n sub dot j" | $n_{\cdot 3} = 20$ High days |
| $\frac{n_{ij}}{n_{i\cdot}}$ | "n sub i j over n sub i dot" — "given row i" | $18/30 = 60\%$ of Sunny days were High |
| $\frac{n_{ij}}{n_{\cdot j}}$ | "n sub i j over n sub dot j" — "given column j" | $18/20 = 90\%$ of High days were Sunny |

**Whole formula as a sentence:** "the conditional share is the count
in one cell divided by the total of the row (or column) you are
restricting to — not by the grand total."
:::

### Scatter plot

When both variables are **quantitative**, grouping them into classes
throws information away. Plot the raw pairs instead.

**Try it.** Five days from the same truck (a simplified extract):
temperature $x$ and number of items sold $y$.

| Day | Temperature $x$ (°C) | Items sold $y$ | $x$ above its mean? | $y$ above its mean? |
|---|---:|---:|---|---|
| 1 | 12 | 40 | ? | ? |
| 2 | 16 | 55 | ? | ? |
| 3 | 21 | 50 | ? | ? |
| 4 | 24 | 70 | ? | ? |
| 5 | 27 | 85 | ? | ? |
| **Total** | **?** | **?** | | |
| **Mean** | **?** | **?** | | |

1. On squared paper, draw an $x$ axis from 10 to 30 °C and a $y$ axis
   from 30 to 90 items. Plot one point per day at $(x, y)$.
2. Compute both means, draw a vertical line at the mean temperature
   and a horizontal line at the mean number of items, then fill the
   last two columns.
3. How many points lie in the lower-left or upper-right quarters of
   the plot? Which day goes against the trend?

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
#### Try it — check your answer
| Day | $x$ (°C) | $y$ | $x$ above 20? | $y$ above 60? |
|---|---:|---:|---|---|
| 1 | 12 | 40 | no | no |
| 2 | 16 | 55 | no | no |
| 3 | 21 | 50 | yes | no |
| 4 | 24 | 70 | yes | yes |
| 5 | 27 | 85 | yes | yes |
| **Total** | **100** | **300** | | |
| **Mean** | **20** | **60** | | |

Four of the five points (Days 1, 2, 4, 5) are in the lower-left or
upper-right quarter: warmer days tend to sell more. Day 3 (21 °C, 50
items) is slightly warmer than average but sells below average — the
points rise to the right, but not along a perfect line.
:::

**See it.** Step 1 of the figure shows the five points; step 2 adds
the two mean lines and colours each point by the quarter it falls in.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
temps = [12, 16, 21, 24, 27]
items = [40, 55, 50, 70, 85]

avg = xs => xs.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0) / xs.length

function quadrants(xs, ys) {
  const mx = avg(xs), my = avg(ys);
  const agree = [], against = [];
  xs.forEach((v, i) =>
    ((v - mx) * (ys[i] - my) > 0 ? agree : against).push(i + 1));
  return {mx, my, agree, against};
}

viewof scatterStep = {
  const labels = ["1 · Points", "2 · Mean lines"];
  const form = html`<form class="ojs-step-picker">Show: ${labels.map((l, i) =>
    html`<label> <input type="radio" name="scatterStep" value="${i + 1}"
      ${i === 0 ? "checked" : ""}> ${l} </label>`)}</form>`;
  form.value = 1;
  form.oninput = () => {
    form.value = +form.querySelector("input:checked").value;
  };
  return form;
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const W = 660, H = 380, L = 60, R = 20, T = 20, B = 50;
  const BLUE = "steelblue", ORANGE = "darkorange";
  const AGREE = "#5cb85c", AGAINST = "#d9534f";
  const x = v => L + (v - 10) * (W - L - R) / (30 - 10);
  const y = v => H - B - (v - 30) * (H - T - B) / (90 - 30);
  const q = quadrants(temps, items);
  let g = "";
  if (scatterStep === 2) {
    g += `<rect x="${x(10)}" y="${y(q.my)}" width="${x(q.mx) - x(10)}"
      height="${y(30) - y(q.my)}" fill="${AGREE}" fill-opacity="0.08"/>`;
    g += `<rect x="${x(q.mx)}" y="${y(90)}" width="${x(30) - x(q.mx)}"
      height="${y(q.my) - y(90)}" fill="${AGREE}" fill-opacity="0.08"/>`;
  }
  for (let t = 10; t <= 30; t += 5) {
    g += `<line x1="${x(t)}" x2="${x(t)}" y1="${y(30)}" y2="${y(90)}"
      stroke="currentColor" stroke-opacity="0.15"/>`;
    g += `<text x="${x(t)}" y="${H - B + 18}" text-anchor="middle"
      fill="currentColor" font-size="12">${t} °C</text>`;
  }
  for (let v = 30; v <= 90; v += 10) {
    g += `<line x1="${x(10)}" x2="${x(30)}" y1="${y(v)}" y2="${y(v)}"
      stroke="currentColor" stroke-opacity="0.15"/>`;
    g += `<text x="${L - 8}" y="${y(v) + 4}" text-anchor="end"
      fill="currentColor" font-size="12">${v}</text>`;
  }
  g += `<text x="${(x(10) + x(30)) / 2}" y="${H - 8}" text-anchor="middle"
    fill="currentColor" font-size="13">Temperature x (°C)</text>`;
  g += `<text x="14" y="${y(60)}" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor"
    font-size="13" transform="rotate(-90 14 ${y(60)})">Items sold y</text>`;
  if (scatterStep === 2) {
    g += `<line x1="${x(q.mx)}" x2="${x(q.mx)}" y1="${y(30)}" y2="${y(90)}"
      stroke="${ORANGE}" stroke-width="2" stroke-dasharray="6 4"/>`;
    g += `<text x="${x(q.mx) + 6}" y="${y(90) + 14}" fill="${ORANGE}"
      font-size="12">mean = ${q.mx} °C</text>`;
    g += `<line x1="${x(10)}" x2="${x(30)}" y1="${y(q.my)}" y2="${y(q.my)}"
      stroke="${ORANGE}" stroke-width="2" stroke-dasharray="6 4"/>`;
    g += `<text x="${x(30) - 4}" y="${y(q.my) - 6}" text-anchor="end"
      fill="${ORANGE}" font-size="12">mean = ${q.my} items</text>`;
  }
  temps.forEach((t, i) => {
    const c = scatterStep === 1 ? BLUE
      : q.agree.includes(i + 1) ? AGREE : AGAINST;
    g += `<circle cx="${x(t)}" cy="${y(items[i])}" r="7" fill="${c}"/>`;
    g += `<text x="${x(t) + 10}" y="${y(items[i]) + 4}" fill="currentColor"
      font-size="12">Day ${i + 1}</text>`;
  });
  return html`<svg viewBox="0 0 ${W} ${H}" width="100%" role="img"
    aria-label="Scatter plot of temperature and items sold for five days">
    ${g}</svg>`;
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const q = quadrants(temps, items);
  const days = ds => ds.map(d => `Day ${d}`).join(", ");
  const text = scatterStep === 1
    ? `Five days from ${Math.min(...temps)} °C to ${Math.max(...temps)} °C and from ${Math.min(...items)} to ${Math.max(...items)} items sold: the cloud rises to the right.`
    : `Means: ${q.mx} °C and ${q.my} items. ${q.agree.length} of ${temps.length} points lie in the lower-left or upper-right quarter (${days(q.agree)}); ${days(q.against)} (${q.against.map(d => `${temps[d - 1]} °C, ${items[d - 1]} items`).join("; ")}) goes against the trend.`;
  return html`<p><em>${text}</em></p>`;
}
```

In plain words: each day becomes a dot at (temperature, revenue). The
cloud of dots shows the pattern — upward trend, downward trend,
curved, or no pattern at all.

::: {.callout-note}
#### Definition — scatter plot
A **scatter plot** places one point per individual, using one
quantitative variable for the $x$-coordinate and another for the
$y$-coordinate. It is the standard first look at a possible
relationship between two quantitative variables, before computing
any numerical summary.
:::

## Worked example

### Contingency table — `weather` × `daily_revenue_eur` class

From "The Wandering Fork"'s Harbour 30-day subset
(`wandering-fork.xlsx`, sheet `harbour_30d`):

| Weather \ Revenue class | [400,500[ | [500,600[ | [600,700[ | [700,800[ | [800,900[ | Row total |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Sunny | 0 | 3 | 6 | 3 | 1 | 13 |
| Cloudy | 3 | 2 | 2 | 3 | 2 | 12 |
| Rainy | 3 | 1 | 0 | 1 | 0 | 5 |
| **Column total** | **6** | **6** | **8** | **7** | **3** | **30** |

**Step 1 — check the margins.** The row totals (13, 12, 5) match
Module 2's `weather` frequency table exactly, and the column totals
(6, 6, 8, 7, 3) match Module 3's `daily_revenue_eur` class table
exactly — both are recovered as marginal distributions of the same
30 rows, confirming the table was built correctly.

**Step 2 — read the pattern.** All 6 days in the lowest revenue class
[400,500[ were either Cloudy or Rainy — zero Sunny days earned under
€500. Conversely, Sunny days account for 10 of the 18 days earning
€600 or more, including 6 of the 8 days in [600,700[. This is a
first, purely visual hint that better weather is associated with
higher revenue.

**Step 3 — conditional distribution.** Restricting to Sunny days
only (row total 13) and rescaling each cell by 13 instead of 30 gives
the *conditional* distribution of revenue class **given Sunny**:
$0\%, 23.1\%, 46.2\%, 23.1\%, 7.7\%$ for the five classes (rounded;
they sum to $100\%$ before rounding) — compare
this to the *unconditional* column percentages from Module 3
(20.0%, 20.0%, 26.7%, 23.3%, 10.0%): Sunny days are visibly shifted
toward the higher revenue classes, confirming the pattern from Step 2
with actual percentages instead of raw counts.

### Scatter plot — `temperature_c` vs `daily_revenue_eur`

Plotting `temperature_c` (x-axis) against `daily_revenue_eur`
(y-axis) for all 30 Harbour days shows points trending upward and to
the right: as temperature rises, revenue tends to rise too, though
the points do not fall on a perfect line — there is visible scatter
around the trend.

## Proof / derivation

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
#### Derivation — marginal totals recover the univariate frequency table (click to expand)
Let $n_{ij}$ be the contingency table's cell counts, with row
modalities $i=1,\dots,r$ and column modalities $j=1,\dots,c$. Every
one of the $n$ individuals is counted in exactly one cell, so summing
across all columns for a fixed row $i$ recovers that row modality's
total univariate count:
$$
n_{i\cdot} = \sum_{j=1}^{c} n_{ij}.
$$
For "The Wandering Fork", row $i=\text{Sunny}$:
$0+3+6+3+1 = 13$, matching Module 2's Sunny count exactly — this is
not a coincidence but a direct consequence of the contingency table
partitioning the same 30 rows both by `weather` and, independently,
by `daily_revenue_eur` class.
:::

## Visual intuition

A contingency table is a two-dimensional histogram: instead of one
row of class counts (Module 3), we now have a *grid* of counts, and
reading down a single column or across a single row projects the
two-dimensional picture back onto one axis — exactly recovering the
one-variable-at-a-time view from Modules 2–3. A scatter plot's
"upward-and-to-the-right" shape is the visual signature of a positive
relationship; Module 9 replaces "shape" with a single number, the
correlation coefficient.

Step 2 of the five-day scatter figure shows where that number comes
from: the two mean lines cut the plot into four quarters, and a
rising cloud puts most points in the lower-left and upper-right
quarters (4 of 5 here). Module 9's covariance adds up exactly this.

## Exercises

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
#### Exercise 1 (by hand) — Reading a contingency table (click for solution)
Out of the 12 Cloudy days, what proportion earned in the top two
revenue classes ([700,800[ or [800,900[)?

**Solution.** Cloudy row: $3+2=5$ days in the top two classes out of
12 Cloudy days total, i.e. $5/12 \approx 41.7\%$.
:::

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
#### Exercise 2 (by hand) — Column margin check (click for solution)
Verify that the column total for [600,700[ (8) is consistent with
Module 3's class frequency table.

**Solution.** Column [600,700[: $6\,(\text{Sunny}) + 2\,(\text{Cloudy})
+ 0\,(\text{Rainy}) = 8$, matching Module 3's $n_{[600,700[}=8$
exactly.
:::

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
#### Exercise 3 (by hand) — Describing a scatter plot (click for solution)
Without computing any number, how would you describe the scatter
plot of `temperature_c` vs. `daily_revenue_eur` — direction, and is
the relationship perfectly linear?

**Solution.** The direction is positive (points trend upward to the
right). The relationship is not perfectly linear — there is visible
scatter of points around any trend line one might draw, meaning
other factors besides temperature also influence daily revenue.
:::

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
#### Exercise 4 (by hand) — Formula to words (click for solution)
Use the Harbour 30-day table of the worked example, with rows
$i = 1$ (Sunny), $2$ (Cloudy), $3$ (Rainy) and columns $j = 1$
([400,500[) to $j = 5$ ([800,900[).

(a) Read $\frac{n_{ij}}{n_{i\cdot}}$ aloud as one sentence. Which
distribution is it?

(b) Compute $n_{3\cdot}$, $n_{\cdot 1}$ and $\frac{n_{31}}{n_{3\cdot}}$,
and say in words what the last number means.

(c) Compute $\frac{n_{31}}{n_{\cdot 1}}$. Why is it different from (b)?

**Solution.** (a) "The count in cell $i$, $j$ divided by the total of
row $i$": the conditional distribution of the column variable given
row modality $i$ (row percentages).
(b) $n_{3\cdot} = 3+1+0+1+0 = 5$ Rainy days; $n_{\cdot 1} = 0+3+3 = 6$
days in [400,500[; $\frac{n_{31}}{n_{3\cdot}} = 3/5 = 60\%$: "60% of
Rainy days earned under €500".
(c) $\frac{n_{31}}{n_{\cdot 1}} = 3/6 = 50\%$: "half of the days under
€500 were Rainy". The cell is the same, but (b) restricts to the
Rainy row and (c) to the [400,500[ column.
:::

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
#### Exercise 5 (by hand) — Words to formula (click for solution)
Use the 50-day table of the hook, with rows $i = 1$ (Sunny), $2$
(Rainy) and columns $j = 1$ (Low), $2$ (Medium), $3$ (High). Write in
symbols, then compute:

(a) "the number of Rainy days with High revenue";
(b) "the share of all days that were Sunny";
(c) "among High days, the share that were Sunny";
(d) "the total number of Medium days, adding down the column".

**Solution.** (a) $n_{23} = 2$.
(b) $\frac{n_{1\cdot}}{n} = 30/50 = 60\%$.
(c) $\frac{n_{13}}{n_{\cdot 3}} = 18/20 = 90\%$.
(d) $n_{\cdot 2} = \sum_i n_{i2} = 9 + 6 = 15$.
:::

## Common mistakes

::: {.callout-warning}
#### Watch out
- **Using raw counts to compare rows with different totals.** Always
  use conditional distributions (% of row/column total) for fair
  comparison.
- **Confusing marginal and conditional distributions.** Marginal =
  overall (ignoring the other variable); conditional = given a
  specific value of the other variable.
- **Reading a scatter plot as proof of causation.** A pattern only
  shows association; Module 9 quantifies the linear association, but
  neither proves causation.
- **Forgetting to group continuous variables for contingency tables.**
  `daily_revenue_eur` must be binned (e.g., €100 classes) before
  crossing with `weather` — PivotTable grouping does this
  automatically.
- **Using a line chart instead of a scatter plot for two quantitative
  variables.** Line charts imply a sequence (time); scatter plots
  show the relationship between two variables measured on the same
  individuals.
:::

## Exit check

Five minutes, no calculator needed except for question 4.

1. In one sentence, what is the difference between a marginal and a
   conditional distribution?
2. Why compare row percentages rather than raw counts when the row
   totals differ?
3. Read $n_{\cdot j} = \sum_i n_{ij}$ aloud as a sentence.
4. Harbour had 12 good days and 8 bad days; Campus had 9 good days and
   21 bad days. Compute the share of good days given each franchise.
5. A scatter plot of temperature and items sold rises to the right.
   Can you conclude that heat causes the extra sales? Why?

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
#### Exit check — answers
1. A marginal distribution describes one variable over all $n$
   individuals, ignoring the other; a conditional distribution
   describes it within one modality of the other variable only.
2. Because a bigger row has bigger counts even when nothing differs:
   in the hook, 9 vs 6 medium days were 30% vs 30%.
3. "The column margin $n_{\cdot j}$ is the sum, over all rows $i$, of
   the counts in column $j$."
4. Harbour: $12/20 = 60\%$; Campus: $9/30 = 30\%$ (row totals 20 and
   30, not the grand total 50).
5. No: a scatter plot only shows association. Other factors (season,
   events, foot traffic) can drive both; Module 9 measures the linear
   association, but neither proves causation.
:::

## Homework — Excel lab

Reproduce, in Excel, every table and chart you built by hand in class,
with `COUNTIFS`, a PivotTable with two fields (and **Show Values As →
% of Row Total**) and an XY scatter chart, then apply them to the full
dataset.

**Estimated time:** about 50–60 minutes. Any spreadsheet application
works, at home or in a campus computer room.

**Follow-up:** a 10-minute debrief at the start of
[Module 9](module-09.qmd). Bring your Step 0 results and any question
on Homework 1–4.

### Using Excel

The sheet `harbour_30d` of `wandering-fork.xlsx` has the data. The
complete list of function names, with their French equivalents, is on
the [Excel functions](excel-functions.qmd) page.

| Concept | Excel function / steps |
|---|---|
| Contingency table | Select the two columns → **Insert → PivotTable**, one variable in Rows, the other in Columns, `Count` in Values |
| Row/column margins | The PivotTable's own "Grand Total" row and column |
| Conditional distribution | In the PivotTable, right-click Values → **Show Values As** → **% of Row Total** (or Column Total) |
| Scatter plot | Select the two quantitative columns → **Insert → Chart → Scatter (X Y)** |
| Two-way `COUNTIFS` | `=COUNTIFS(range1, criterion1, range2, criterion2, …)` for cell counts |

For the **full table** (120 days per franchise) use the Excel Table
`tblFork` and add the franchise as one more condition, for example
`=COUNTIFS(tblFork[franchise],"Harbour",tblFork[weather],"Sunny",tblFork[daily_revenue_eur],">=600",tblFork[daily_revenue_eur],"<700")`.

### Step 0 — check your class results

1. Type the ten-day log of the contingency-table Try it in `A2:B11`
   (column A `Weather`, column B `Revenue level`, headers in row 1).
2. Build the 2×3 table either with a PivotTable (Weather in Rows,
   Revenue level in Columns, Count in Values) or with `COUNTIFS`, e.g.
   `=COUNTIFS($A$2:$A$11,"Sunny",$B$2:$B$11,"High")`, and add the
   margins with `SUM`.
3. Type the 50-day table of the hook (Sunny 3, 9, 18; Rainy 12, 6, 2),
   compute the row totals with `SUM`, and the row percentages by
   dividing each cell by its row total (e.g. `=E2/$H2` if the counts
   are in `E2:G3` and the totals in `H2:H3`), formatted as a
   percentage.
4. Type the five (temperature, items sold) pairs in two columns, insert
   a **Scatter (X Y)** chart, and compute both means with `AVERAGE`.
5. Compare every result with your hand computation.

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
#### Step 0 — expected results
| Ten-day table | Low | Medium | High | Row total |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Sunny | 1 | 2 | 3 | 6 |
| Rainy | 2 | 1 | 1 | 4 |
| Column total | 3 | 3 | 4 | 10 |

| 50-day table, % of Row Total | Low | Medium | High | Row total |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Sunny | 10% | 30% | 60% | 30 days |
| Rainy | 60% | 30% | 10% | 20 days |
| Grand total (% of all days) | 30% | 30% | 40% | 50 days |

Scatter plot: five points rising to the right; `AVERAGE` gives 20 °C
and 60 items. If the chart looks wrong, check that temperature is the
left-hand column (Excel uses it for the $x$ axis).
:::

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
#### Homework 1 (Excel) — Build the contingency table for Campus (click for solution)
In `wandering-fork.xlsx`, filter `franchise` to "Campus" and build a
PivotTable crossing `weather` (Rows) with `daily_revenue_eur` class
(Columns, grouped in €100 bins). What are the row totals? Do they
match Module 2's Campus `weather` frequencies?

**How to.** Insert a PivotTable on `tblFork`, put `franchise` in
Filters (select Campus), `weather` in Rows and `daily_revenue_eur` in
Columns, then right-click a revenue label → **Group…** with By = 100.

**Solution.** Campus 120-day row totals: Sunny 50, Cloudy 48, Rainy
22 (total 120). These match the Campus `weather` frequencies from
Module 2 (Sunny 41.7%, Cloudy 40.0%, Rainy 18.3%).
:::

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
#### Homework 2 (Excel) — Conditional distribution: revenue given promo (click for solution)
Using the full 240-row `tblFork`, build a PivotTable with `promo_active`
(Rows) and `daily_revenue_eur` class (Columns, €100 bins). Show
values as **% of Row Total**. Compare the conditional distributions
for "Yes" vs "No" promo. Is revenue higher when a promo is active?

**How to.** Same PivotTable as Homework 1 without the franchise
filter, `promo_active` in Rows; right-click a value → **Show Values
As → % of Row Total**, then add up the classes below €200, from €400
and from €600.

**Solution.** There are 26 promo days and 214 non-promo days. Summing
the row percentages: below €200, 15.4% (Yes) vs 19.2% (No); €400 or
more, 53.8% vs 48.1%; €600 or more, 23.1% vs 23.4%. Promo days have
slightly less mass in the lowest classes, but the top of the two
distributions is almost identical. The difference is small and rests
on only 26 days — and it is descriptive, not causal (other factors
may drive both promo and revenue).
:::

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
#### Homework 3 (Excel) — Scatter plot: foot traffic vs revenue (click for solution)
Create a scatter plot of `foot_traffic` (x) vs `daily_revenue_eur` (y)
for Harbour 120 days. Describe the direction, form, and strength of
the pattern.

**How to.** Filter `tblFork` to Harbour, select `foot_traffic` then
`daily_revenue_eur` (x column first), and choose **Insert → Chart →
Scatter (X Y)**.

**Solution.** Strong positive linear trend: more foot traffic
clearly associates with higher revenue. The points cluster tightly
around an upward line — much tighter than temperature vs revenue.
This visually confirms the $r \ge 0.80$ correlation from the dataset
design.
:::

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
#### Homework 4 (Excel) — Harbour vs Campus: weather and revenue (click for solution)
For each franchise (120 days each), compute the conditional share of
days with `daily_revenue_eur` of €500 or more **given** each
`weather` category. Is the weather–revenue association equally strong
at both trucks?

**How to.** Lay out a 3×2 grid (weather × franchise) and fill each
cell with the formula below, changing "Harbour" and "Sunny" each time
(or pointing to the row and column header cells).

**Solution.** For Harbour and Sunny:

```text
=COUNTIFS(tblFork[franchise],"Harbour",tblFork[weather],"Sunny",
          tblFork[daily_revenue_eur],">=500")
 /COUNTIFS(tblFork[franchise],"Harbour",tblFork[weather],"Sunny")
```

| Weather | Harbour | Campus |
|---|---:|---:|
| Sunny | 25/53 = 47.2% | 19/50 = 38.0% |
| Cloudy | 11/42 = 26.2% | 18/48 = 37.5% |
| Rainy | 2/25 = 8.0% | 6/22 = 27.3% |

At Harbour the share falls sharply from Sunny to Rainy (47.2% to
8.0%): weather is strongly associated with revenue. At Campus the
three shares are much closer (38.0%, 37.5%, 27.3%): the association
is weaker, so other factors (such as nearby events) matter more
there.
:::
